purpose: Naloxone is an emergency medicine used to rapidly reverse an opioid overdose. It can save a life when someone has taken too much of an opioid drug like heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, or morphine and has stopped breathing or is unresponsive. It is meant to be used right away in an emergency while you wait for help to arrive.
how_it_works: Opioids work by attaching to special receptors in your brain that slow down your breathing. Naloxone works by quickly pushing the opioid off those receptors and blocking them, which reverses the dangerous effects almost immediately. Think of it like a key that kicks the opioid out and takes its place, allowing the person to breathe normally again within minutes.
common_side_effects: Because naloxone reverses the opioid so quickly, it may cause sudden withdrawal symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, sweating, shaking, irritability, rapid heartbeat, or increased blood pressure. The person may also wake up feeling confused, anxious, or agitated. These effects are temporary and are actually a sign the medicine is working.
warnings: Naloxone wears off in 30 to 90 minutes, which may be shorter than the opioid still in the body — this means the overdose can return and the person may stop breathing again. Always call 911 immediately and stay with the person even after giving naloxone. A second or third dose may be needed, especially with powerful opioids like fentanyl. Naloxone does not work on overdoses caused by alcohol, benzodiazepines, or other non-opioid drugs.
typical_dosing: For the nasal spray (Narcan): Spray one dose into one nostril. If the person does not respond after 2 to 3 minutes, give a second dose in the other nostril. Repeat every 2 to 3 minutes if needed until help arrives. For the auto-injector: Follow the voice instructions on the device and inject into the outer thigh. Always call 911 first or have someone else call while you give the medicine.
